officialTitle: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

meaning.text: No scheduled sunset for these higher rates. Voters can still amend the Constitution; the Legislature can propose an amendment with two-thirds of each house, subject to voter approval. No fixed yearly revenue is guaranteed.

evidence.locator: Sec. 4, Article XIII §36(f)(2)–(3): removal of expiration, pp. 114–115

amount.text: The analyst projects continued annual revenue, varying with the stock market:

scope.period: future years after the scheduled sunset

comparison.reason: The captured guide does not provide matching future-year General Fund budgets; a current-year spending figure is not the future budget denominator.

comparison.text: The captured guide does not provide a matching future-year budget denominator. Revenue varies with the stock market; this projection does not establish its future budget share.

questions.question: How much stability does continuing a volatile tax buy?

path.text: Compare the revenue range with the spending commitments and reserve rules in the analyst’s fiscal discussion.

takeaway.text: “Permanent” removes the scheduled end of higher tax rates. It does not lock in a yearly funding amount or prevent a later constitutional amendment.

today.text: Higher income-tax rates apply through 2030, then expire. These rates are paid by the top 2% of California taxpayers.

change.text: Proposition 3 removes the 2031 expiration of the higher rates; it continues an existing tax rather than creating a tax on everyone.

evidence.locator: Sec. 4, Article XIII §36(f)(2)–(3), pp. 114–115: struck expiration clauses

rationale.text: The measure’s findings say ending the higher rates would reduce resources for education and health care. This is its stated reason; it is not evidence that every additional dollar improves services.

action.text: Continuing the higher rates preserves revenue after their scheduled expiration. The amount depends heavily on high-income earnings and investment gains.
The analyst estimates roughly 40% of added funding goes to schools and community colleges; the remainder supports other state programs, with part set aside in reserves.

tradeoffs.text: Continuing revenue supports public services, while high-income taxpayers continue paying rates that would otherwise expire. Revenue still fluctuates with investment gains.

claim.text: A continuing tax is not a promise of the same dollars every year. Future revenue and program outcomes cannot be read from the word “permanent.”

mechanismQuestion: How does continuing the tax affect funding?

officialTitle: PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

sources.name: California State Auditor: authority and work

meaning.text: The state must supply an eligible voter an ID card on request without an issuance charge. The text does not specify supporting documents, travel, processing time or replacement steps. No fee does not mean no practical cost.

amount.text: The analyst projects the following annual state and local costs:

money.nominal: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars

comparison.reason: The estimate combines state and local costs; the state General Fund alone is not a matching denominator, and county-level budgets and cost allocations are not supplied.

comparison.text: The analyst’s statewide scale comparison does not establish a matched state-and-local budget share or show the burden on each county or voter.

finding.text: The auditor found gaps in consistent cost and outcome information and recommended state reporting changes.

evidence.locator: Recommendations to Legislature and Cal ICH

followThrough.text: Cal ICH’s response agreed with recommendations and described intended improvements. Agreement is not evidence that all recommended changes were implemented.

outcome.text: This captured report does not verify realized savings resulting from the recommendations. It is evidence of a finding and response, not a measured return on auditing.

limit.text: Homelessness reporting is a different program. This example shows why follow-through matters, not whether election audits would work.

finding.text: The auditor identified 191 recommendations to 46 nonstate entities that were more than a year old and not fully implemented.

followThrough.text: The report tracks unimplemented recommendations and follow-up. It does not say all agencies ignored every finding.

outcome.text: An unimplemented-recommendation count is not an estimate of money wasted or a success rate for all audits.

limit.text: The 191 overdue recommendations came from 632 recommendations in 63 reports involving nonstate entities issued November 2017–October 2022. This historical set cannot predict Proposition 39 outcomes.

evidence.locator: Results in brief: nonstate entities; cohort and timeframe

finding.text: The auditor found inaccurate tobacco-tax rates and recommended updating the data source.

evidence.locator: Letter to Governor and Legislature; introduction

followThrough.text: The tax agency changed its calculation method. The auditor’s follow-up reported additional annual tax revenue:

comparison.reason: The captured follow-up does not provide a matched annual state revenue budget for this 2022 result or net implementation costs. This is additional revenue, not net audit savings.

outcome.text: This is auditor-reported revenue from a changed calculation, not an audited estimate of net savings after the cost of conducting the audit.

limit.text: Tax administration differs from election compliance. This example supports investigating follow-through, not a claim that Proposition 39 would produce similar revenue or benefits.

claim.text: Today, a missing or nonmatching signature has a correction process through the county. The proposal adds the ID-number check; the existing signature correction procedure does not establish a remedy for a new ID-number error.

scenarios.title: I do not have an ID

claim.text: You could request the promised free voter ID. Required documents, application access and processing time remain unspecified in the measure, so practical steps cannot yet be listed.

questions.question: Which problems would the check address, and how often do they occur?

path.text: Start with the measure’s stated goals; seek independent evidence distinguishing impersonation, registration errors and other fraud before judging the likely benefit.

questions.question: Who would fix an error, and by when?

path.text: Inspect the future implementing laws and county instructions for ID correction, deadlines, accessibility and fallback procedures. The measure does not supply these details.

takeaway.text: Proposition 39 adds an ID check at each vote. Its audits produce public findings and recommendations; changes still require action by officials, lawmakers or courts.

today.text: Identity is checked during registration. In person, voters typically sign the voter list; some first-time voters must show ID. Mail voters sign the envelope, and officials compare the signature.

change.text: In person: present government-issued ID. By mail: write the last four digits of the selected government-issued ID number on the envelope, matching registration. Identity must be verified before a regular or provisional ballot counts.

rationale.text: The measure states goals of public confidence, detecting fraud and reducing impersonation. Its text describes the proposed checks; it does not measure how common each problem is or how much fraud they would prevent.

action.text: State and county officials must implement the ID checks and make best efforts to verify citizenship using government data.
In each odd-numbered year the auditor reviews state and county compliance and publishes findings and recommendations. This clause grants no power to issue ballot-counting orders or impose penalties.

chain.actor: Officials, Legislature and courts · act next

action.text: Officials must comply; the Legislature must promptly pass implementation laws. Citizens may seek judicial review and remedy.
An audit can expose noncompliance. Improvement depends on corrective action and workable implementation; an ignored recommendation is not itself a correction.

evidence.locator: How our work begins: public reports, hearings and legislation

tradeoffs.text: The additional checks aim to verify who casts a ballot, while adding steps for voters and administrators. The pilot has no verified estimate of present impersonation prevalence or the number of eligible voters affected.

Mail envelopes would carry four digits, not a full identifier. The text does not specify shielding from observers or establish actual misuse; privacy risk depends on handling and other information an observer has.

claim.text: Which specific IDs qualify is unresolved. The analyst says the Legislature must clarify this; do not assume a passport, birth certificate or current license will qualify.

evidence.locator: Requires legislative action for full implementation

claim.text: The text does not detail how to correct a wrong ID number, missing ID, name mismatch or delays receiving a free card. It requires verification even for provisional ballots; this pilot cannot establish a cure deadline.
The guide gives a total implementation estimate, not an isolated audit cost or a measured benefit from these proposed audits. Value for money cannot be calculated from this evidence.

officialTitle: INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

claim.text: Illustration in 2027–28: assume the annual tax revenues, opening reserve and otherwise-required deposit shown below, with no capital-gains addition, adjustments or emergency. The old 10% cap blocks the deposit; the new 20% cap permits it. The deposit changes destination, not total revenue.

evidence.locator: Article XVI, section 20(a)(2); assumed amounts illustrate the rule, not a forecast

comparison.reason: This is a reserve stock, not annual spending. It equals the old 10% tax-revenue cap in the example; a matching stock budget denominator is inapplicable.

evidence.locator: Article XVI, section 20(a)(2); assumed amounts illustrate the rule, not a forecast

claim.text: With the same figures but a fully suspended transfer during a budget emergency, neither rule requires the deposit shown below. Raising the cap would not increase this year’s reserve balance.

evidence.locator: Article XVI, section 20(a)(2); assumed amounts illustrate the rule, not a forecast

questions.question: What would receive less money in order to save more?

path.text: Trace the cap’s infrastructure diversion and the debt-payment split, then compare the value of spending now with a larger reserve for future shortfalls.

takeaway.text: A higher reserve cap allows more saving; it does not create money. Required deposits would continue longer, using revenue that could otherwise go to infrastructure.

today.text: The rainy-day fund generally receives 0.75% of General Fund tax revenue plus deposits tied to unusually high investment gains. At the 10% balance limit, money otherwise deposited goes to infrastructure.

change.text: The measure raises the transfer limit to 20%, increases the investment-gain formula above a threshold and extends extra debt-payment rules through 2039–40. Transfers remain subject to budget-emergency reductions.

rationale.text: The Legislature’s findings say more reserves can cushion revenue downturns. Whether spending cuts are avoided depends on the amount saved and the size of a later shortfall.

action.text: Finance estimates tax revenue and capital-gains revenue in the Budget Act. The changed formula counts 150% of capital-gains tax revenue above 10% of General Fund taxes, with specified offsets.
The Controller transfers money from the General Fund into the reserve account under Finance’s schedule. The cap rises from 10% to 20%; money blocked by the cap otherwise goes to infrastructure.
Half the calculated amount is reserved for specified obligations through 2039–40. During a budget emergency, deposits can be suspended or reduced; withdrawals can lower the balance.
When required deposits would exceed the old cap but fit below the new cap, more can be saved instead of directed to infrastructure. A larger cap alone adds nothing if deposits are suspended.

tradeoffs.text: Saving revenue now can help pay for programs in a downturn, while leaving less for infrastructure when the old cap would have redirected deposits there. These are competing uses of the same dollars.
Extending the debt-payment split can divert money that could otherwise be fully deposited after 2030 under current law. The net balance depends on revenue, the cap and discretionary debt choices.

claim.text: Future balances depend on revenues, debt allocations and withdrawals. The source establishes changed rules, not an exact dollar increase in reserves.
